content.thinking:
I'm planning a whimsical barnstormer biplane design at realistic scale, roughly 6 meters long with a 7.5 meter wingspan, featuring a chubby round fuselage, oversized cowling and wheels, and a cheerful cream, red, and teal color scheme, all built carefully in one pass with familiar APIs.

For the skeleton, I'm sketching joints for the propeller hinge, rudder, elevators, ailerons, and wheel axles rooted at the fuselage, keeping the hierarchy simple to avoid unused-import errors. I'm working out the fuselage layout along the z-axis from tail to nose, placing the lower wing near the fuselage and the upper wing above on struts, and extruding the wing shape from a top-view outline with rounded tips to get that classic biplane silhouette.

I'm designing the wing surface paint with rib stripes, a cream wingtip band, and a darker leading edge, wrapped in a cel-shaded paint function, then setting up separate hinged aileron parts on the upper wing's trailing edge.

Now I'm defining how joints inherit parent bones by default and specifying body explicitly where needed, then building the fuselage as a lofted shape along stations from tail to nose with varying width, height, and vertical offset to give it a whimsical, chubby profile, followed by a lathe-based rounded nose cowling.

I'm shaping the cowling profile and thinking through coloring: using cel-shaded red with a countershaded cream belly, plus a racing stripe or number decal planned for the fuselage sides.

For the roundel decal, I'll skip trying to render text and instead draw a star inside a circle with stripes, oriented correctly on both sides of the fuselage. Then I'm adding two whimsical open cockpits as dark flattened ellipse openings on top of the fuselage.

Writing cockpit geometry...

Now for the pilot: I'll give them a helmet, goggles, and a long whimsical scarf streaming back, placed in the rear cockpit. For the front seat I'm thinking of adding a small whimsical passenger—maybe a round teddy bear or bunny made of simple sphere shapes for the body, head, and ears. I'll also detail the engine cowling with small cylinder bumps arranged radially to suggest a round engine.

Now I'm shaping the propeller: a spinner cone at the hub, with two blades built from extruded outlines mirrored 180 degrees about the hinge, their tips painted yellow against a wood-colored base. I'm also working out the wing placement, positioning the lower wing so it meets the bottom of the fuselage.

I'm reworking the positioning of the wings and cabane struts relative to the cockpits, trying to figure out the right z-coordinates so the front and rear cockpits don't collide with the strut mounts.

Positioning pilot and passenger cockpits at z=-0.95 and z=-0.35, with cabane struts running from the fuselage up to the upper wing and interplane struts connecting the lower wing to the upper wing at front and rear positions.

Now I'm adding diagonal flying wires between the wings, outer strut pairs further out along the span, and wood-toned coloring for the struts, then starting on the V-shaped landing gear struts running from the fuselage bottom down to the axle.

For the wheels, I'm placing an axle rod across the fuselage width, then building each wheel from a torus rotated to lie flat in the correct plane, with a hub disc cylinder in cream/red, and setting up a hinge joint at each wheel position for rotation.

For the tail, I'm adding a skid strut running from the fuselage down to a small tail wheel sphere near the ground, with a vertical fin extruded as an outline shape in the z-y plane at the rear of the model.

Still defining fin coordinates...

Setting the hinge joint position and orientation for the rudder, then laying out the horizontal stabilizer with separate hinged elevators behind it, working out their span, chord, and z-positions relative to the tail center.

Defining the elevator outline shape...

Still defining wing outline points...

For ailerons I'm thinking of placing them as separate extrusions trailing behind the main wing rather than cutting into the wing mesh, shifting their y-range further back to avoid overlap.

Settling on a simplified trapezoid shape for the aileron outline, then shifting focus to the main wing geometry, setting up the upper wing's y-range and z-origin for the next section of coordinates.

Working out the lower wing dimensions to mirror the upper wing's chord, and the wing thickness and beveling, along with strut positions connecting the two. Now I'm defining a wing paint function to add rib lines, leading edge bands, and tip coloring for visual detail.

Applying a two-tone scheme with base red and cream tips, with darker rib lines spaced periodically along the span, and making sure the shading works correctly on the extruded side walls and underside. I'm also double-checking that I'm staying within the flat color budget.

Settling on a cheerful palette — red, cream, teal, yellow, wood, dark, leather, metal, navy — and deciding the fuselage will be teal on top with a cream countershaded belly, wings in red/cream, and a red cowling.

Writing paint logic for a yellow stripe band...

I'm now planning rivet details using merged sphere geometries placed in rings around the cowling front, roughly 16 small spheres per ring positioned along the cowling radius.

Working out rivet placement at radius 0.51 with small sunken spheres, and setting the lathe axis along z for the cowling with red paint following the surface normals. Now moving on to shaping the radial engine cylinders.

For the front cowling, I'm deciding to keep the dome and spinner at z 1.65, skip separate cylinders, and instead add exhaust stubs as short metal capsules sweeping from the cowling sides back toward the fuselage, three per side. I'm building the spinner as a lathed cone positioned at the propeller joint, figuring out the outline profile and where blades attach relative to the spinner's base disk and the joint coordinates.

Now I'm shaping each propeller blade as an extruded outline with a tapered, slightly rounded tip painted yellow, mirroring the second blade across the opposite axis, and checking that the two-meter-plus diameter prop clears the ground. I'm also planning small tinted windscreens as thin tilted glass boxes in front of the cockpit, positioning them carefully to avoid colliding with the cabane strut.

Then I'm adding a leather-colored torus rim around each cockpit opening, scaling it before rotation so it reads as an elongated ellipse rather than a perfect circle, and cutting a dark recessed cylinder into the center to represent the open cockpit hole.

I'm checking that the rim height lines up with the fuselage's curved top surface at both cockpit positions, adjusting the y-coordinate so the torus and dark disc sit flush rather than floating or sinking into the hull. Then I'm starting on the seated pilot figure for the rear cockpit, building the torso as an ellipsoid that pokes up visibly above the rim.

Adding pilot head, goggles, helmet...

Plotting out the control points for the wavy ribbon path with a slight x-axis wiggle, orienting the sweep section using an up vector along x.

I'll default the bone assignment to body for parts and sweeps, specifying it explicitly to avoid ambiguity with nearest-joint logic. Now I'm designing the teddy bear passenger in the front cockpit—a brown sphere body and head, rounded ears, a muzzle, dark nose and eyes, a red bow tie, and small capsule arms raised in a wave—then placing a windscreen just in front of it, sized to clear the teddy's head height.

For whimsy, I want to give the plane a face too, with two googly eyes painted onto the cowling—white spheres with dark pupils positioned near the front dome's upper corners, angled slightly forward and outward to feel playful. I'm working out the geometry of where these eye decals should sit on the curved cowling surface.

Mirroring the eye isn't needed since it's symmetrical, and I'll skip brows, cheeks, and a smile to keep it simple. I'm also adding a roundel decal to the top surface of each wing, positioned near the wing's upper edge and sized proportionally.

For the tail, I'll paint the rudder with red/cream/navy stripes using coordinate-based banding instead of decals. On the fuselage, I'm skipping text (too risky with unknown fonts) and instead placing a star roundel decal on the side, positioning it based on the fuselage's tapered width at that height.

Rather than a trailing banner, I think a small bunting garland strung between the wing struts would be a nicer whimsical touch -- triangular flags sagging along a wire between the interplane struts.

Still shaping the pennant triangles...

Working out strut placement with two pairs per side at x=1.7 and 3.2, running vertical struts between the wings, then adding diagonal brace wires across each bay for rigidity. I'm keeping the inner bay near the cabane simpler for now, planning the cross-bracing wires there separately.

Positioning the cabane struts to connect the fuselage top to the upper wing root, front and rear sets, keeping them inboard within the fuselage width. Now thinking about strut cross-section -- should streamline them as flattened rods rather than plain cylinders for a more realistic biplane look.

Skipping the walkway and rib bands for simplicity, I'll add tail bracing wires running from the fin top down to the stabilizer ends.

A small tail wheel needs a sphere with a dark leather-like finish, attached to a strut connecting to the fuselage bottom, and I'm working out the gear strut geometry forming a V shape at the front.

I'll skip fenders and wheel pants to keep things simple, and add a red cylindrical shock absorber on the strut plus a cream hub with hubcap at the wheel center.

Now I'm building the tire geometry and hub spokes using thin crossed boxes rotated to form a plus-shape, then setting up the joint hierarchy with the fuselage as root, attaching the propeller, wheels, rudder, and control surfaces with appropriate roles and positions.

I settle on nine joints total, defining wheelL on the +X side with the axle positioned so the tire bottom just touches the ground. I check overall height for proportions, confirming the fin, upper wing, and pilot head positions keep the model around 2.5 units tall, consistent with a biplane scale.

Length comes to about 5.1m nose to tail and wingspan 7.4m, a whimsical compression of the real Stearman proportions. I need to make sure the outline arrays passed to extrude are typed correctly as OutlinePoint[] rather than inferred as plain number[][], and double-check the mergeGeometries import path works with the addon types. I'm writing a helper function to merge sphere geometries at given points for rivet details, translating each sphere to its target position before combining them into one buffer geometry.

For the cowling, I'm setting up a lathe shape with an outline that starts and ends on the axis, using a painted coloring function that maps a yellow stripe band onto the red cowling body based on the lathe's height parameter.

Now I'm working out the spinner geometry as a lathe shape placed at the front of the cowling, planning out the axial positions so the cowling dome, spinner base, and spinner tip line up correctly along the fuselage.

For the eye decals, I'm computing placement coordinates on the curved cowling surface using the sphere's radius equation to find matching x/y positions, and setting slight outward-facing directions so the left and right eyes mirror each other properly.

Writing eye SVG...

Working through the cross product, forward direction (+z) ends up pointing left for the viewer, so the pupil should sit toward cx 24 on the left side where direction is +x. I need to apply the mirrored logic for the right side where direction is -x.

Now I'm designing the roundel emblem using nested circles in navy, cream, and red, topped with a star shape to give it a playful sun-like look within a 100x100 viewBox.

I'm figuring out the fuselage body shape by defining a series of cross-section stations from tail to nose, each with its own width and height, so the loft produces a tapered, rounded fuselage with a pointed tail and a fuller nose section.

I need to make sure the cockpit openings, windscreens, and pilot torso positions line up with the top of the fuselage curve, and that the wing strut attachment points sit just inside the belly line where the fuselage narrows. I also want to double check that the upper and lower wings intersect the fuselage at sensible heights before setting up the shared color palette for the cel-shaded style.

I'm defining thin rod geometry for the wire struts with a low radius and four-sided cross-section to keep them lightweight, and building both wings as single beveled extrusions attached to the body with their airfoil-like outline coordinates.

Now I'm writing the paint logic for the wing surface, using distance-from-center checks to apply cream trim near the tips, darker red leading edges, and subtle rib striping across the fabric, wrapped with the cel-shading function.

Writing wing color scheme...

Making stabilizer and fin solid teal, then working out the rudder and fin geometry and their coordinate orientations to position the outline correctly.

Checking the vertical rudder/fin top alignment confirms a match. Now I'm defining the horizontal stabilizer geometry at z≈-2.55, setting its outline points, smoothing, and thickness, though I need to double check the z-depth range for proper fit against the tail.

Next I'm working out the elevator shape attached behind the stabilizer, placing its joint near center so left and right elevators nearly meet, then painting the stabilizer with the teal material. For the ailerons, I'm positioning their joints near the trailing edge of the upper wing where it aligns at z=0, defining their outline, and noting that only the upper wing gets ailerons while the lower wing does not.

Now I'm adding small decorative touches: skipping the pitot tube and headlights, but adding tiny navigation light spheres at the lower wingtips and considering a whimsical rubber-duck mascot ornament on top of the cowling, built from small spheres for the body and head plus a cone or box beak, sized to sit just above the cowling's radius. I'm also deciding to skip the horn and wing-walker details, and confirming the card setup imports the frame module correctly.

I'm planning the bunting strings draped between the wings using a Catmull-Rom curve through three points on each side, swept into thin cream-colored cords, with small pennant flags placed as cards along the path at even intervals, oriented using frames derived from the curve and sized to hang naturally downward from their attachment points.

For the pennants, I'm generating four colored SVG textures (red, yellow, cream, navy) procedurally and sampling randomly among them. Then I'm shifting to the windscreens, calculating a backward tilt rotation on the box geometry so the top leans toward negative z, with a light blue color and a slightly larger dark frame box behind it for a rim effect.

Now I'm working out the pilot's goggles and cap: cylindrical lenses tilted to face forward, positioned against the head sphere, with a torus strap wrapping around for the goggle band, and a hemisphere cap in leather color sitting on top of the head.

Adding details for the earflaps, nose bump, cheeks, and a red torus scarf wrapped around the neck, plus the pilot's torso as a scaled sphere in a brownish leather jacket tone.

Now I'm positioning the control stick as a small rod with a knob, then adding arm rods connecting the shoulders to the stick for a gripping pose. I'm also checking that each cockpit's windscreen sits correctly in front of its occupant, matching windscreen z-positions to the passenger and pilot seats.

I'm working through the opening geometry, realizing the pilot and passenger cockpit openings overlap, so I shift the passenger seat to z=-0.35 and move the pilot back to z=-1.05 to keep their torus openings separate. Then I'm placing the windscreens accordingly—one near the shared edge around z=-0.70 and the passenger one near the cabane rear struts around z=-0.02.

Now I'm sketching out the teddy bear mascot: a brown sphere body and head with small ears, a cream muzzle, dark eyes and nose, a red bow tie, and raised capsule arms, positioned near the pilot's seat.

Writing exhaust pipe sweeps...

I'm also planning a panel decal for the fuselage side — a small SVG with a stroked rectangle, rivets, and a handle to suggest a fuel hatch, positioned near the passenger area.

I'm then thinking about adding a star roundel decal near the nose, checking that its size fits within the fuselage's narrower width at that point along the body.

Now I'm planning additional surface details like propeller hub bolts, cowl rivets, and strut bolts, then setting up the export metadata and starting the builder code.

Writing builder setup code...

Renaming variables to avoid shadowing, then setting up a ball helper for sphere parts with configurable radius, color, position, and scale, bound to the body joint. Now I'm starting to build the wheel joints, looping over left and right sides.

Still writing wheel geometry...

Tread blocks using tube UV for stripes seem sufficient, so I'll skip shock absorber cylinders and just add merged sphere collars instead. I'm importing toon and glow helpers for nav lights and a landing lamp, collecting bolt positions into an array, and continuing to write the rod/strut geometry.

Checking through remaining details: a star-polygon helper function, skipping tail panel lines, setting decal orientation per surface (up vector varies by wing versus fuselage), and verifying imports are all correct before finalizing the file.
